gist: Someone asks how long fish live and the answer reads 'long' as fish length, saying probably the same as short ones.

characters.looks: curious man, casual sweater, holding a fishing rod

wordplay.explanation: German 'wie lange' (how long, duration) is read as 'lange Fische' (long fish), so the answer compares them with short fish.

ru.note: Russian 'как долго' and 'длинные' do not overlap.

en.note: Pun survives literally: 'How long do fish live? Same as short ones.'

gist: Old woman says her first time was 'at 18', and her friend, reading it as 'with 18', primly says hers was with just one.

en.note: English 'at 18' is not ambiguous; needs a new age/number double meaning.

gist: Roommate caught using someone's deodorant says he is Robin Hood who steals it and distributes it 'unter den Armen', meaning both among the poor and under the arms.

characters.looks: annoyed young man, towel on shoulder, holding empty deodorant
young man, raised arms, cheeky grin

wordplay.explanation: German 'unter den Armen' means 'among the poor' (Robin Hood) and 'under the arms' (deodorant).

ru.note: No Russian word for both poor and armpits.

en.note: Use the alms/arms homophone, e.g. 'I give arms to the poor'.

gist: Man at a prostate exam gets creepy hints from the doctor; told he may get an erection, he says he isn't gay, and the doctor says he meant himself.

gist: Friend asks if a girlfriend screams when she 'comes', and the answer takes it as arriving home: no, she has a key.

wordplay.explanation: German 'kommen' means both to orgasm and to arrive home.

ru.note: Russian 'кончать' and 'приходить' are different words.

en.note: English 'come' carries both meanings.

gist: A wife's way of presenting her husband degrades over the years via 'vorstellen': introducing him, then 'can you imagine', then asking someone to stand in front of him.

man ageing over time, growing belly, sloppy clothes

wordplay.explanation: German 'vorstellen' means to introduce and 'sich vorstellen' to imagine; 'sich davor stellen' means to stand in front of (to hide him).

ru.note: 'Представить' covers introduce/imagine; invent a third step like 'заслоните его'.

en.note: Needs a new three-step phrase chain, e.g. 'meet my husband' / 'can you believe my husband' / 'stand in front of my husband'.

gist: A mute man tells a deaf man that the blind man is watching them, an absurd chain of impossible senses.

characters.looks: man, finger to lips, suspicious glance
man, hearing aid, leaning in
man, dark glasses, white cane

gist: Two chocolate bars fall off a shelf; one broke two 'ribs' (segments), the other landed on its 'nuts', meaning nut filling and testicles.

characters.looks: cartoon chocolate bar, cracked segments, pained face
cartoon hazelnut chocolate bar, wheezing, eyes crossed

wordplay.explanation: 'Rippen' are both ribs and chocolate segments; 'Nüsse' are both nuts in the chocolate and slang for testicles.

ru.note: Russian 'орехи' lacks the testicle sense; rework the pun.

en.note: 'Nuts' works in English; replace 'ribs' with 'pieces' or 'squares'.

gist: Children's riddle: don't enter the jungle at noon because elephants practise skydiving then, which is why crocodiles are flat.

characters.looks: cartoon elephant with parachute and goggles

gist: Vampire on a tandem bike is asked by a cop if he has been drinking and says yes, two 'Radler', meaning both shandies and cyclists.

characters.looks: pale man, black cape, fangs, satisfied grin
police officer, uniform, cap, breathalyzer

wordplay.explanation: German 'Radler' is both a beer-lemonade drink and a cyclist, so the vampire drank two cyclists.

cultureRefs: Radler is a German beer-and-lemonade drink

ru.note: Literal 'двух велосипедистов' keeps the vampire joke but loses the drink pun.

en.note: Literal 'two cyclists' keeps the vampire joke but loses the shandy pun.

gist: Father explains his daughters were named after the flowers they were conceived on, then tells his son the parents were already banned from the park when he was conceived.

characters.looks: middle-aged man, cardigan, armchair, embarrassed smile
girl, pigtails, rose hairclip
younger girl, lily-print dress
small boy, striped shirt, curious

ru.note: Rosa/Lilia become Роза/Лилия; keep a plain non-flower name for the son.

en.note: Rosa/Lilia become Rose/Lily; keep a plain non-flower name for the son.

gist: Not a joke: a student asks online for a joke about the Catholic Church to earn bonus points on homework.

characters.looks: teenager, hoodie, laptop, pleading face

gist: Germany's best-selling bread roll is 'that one', followed by 'no, the one next to it', mocking how people order by pointing.

characters.looks: shopper pointing at bakery display, unsure
baker, white apron, tongs in hand

cultureRefs: German bakeries sell dozens of bread roll varieties

ru.note: Can say 'bakery item' or 'pastry' instead of Brötchen.

en.note: Can say 'bakery item' instead of bread roll.

gist: Riddle: what goes 100 km/h and has only 23 teeth? A bus trip from the retirement home.

characters.looks: toothless grinning old man in bus seat

en.note: Use 60 mph for US audience.

gist: Magician who saws people in half is asked if he has siblings and says yes, two half-sisters.

characters.looks: man in tailcoat and top hat, thin mustache
party guest, glass of wine, polite smile

wordplay.explanation: 'Halbschwestern' means half-sisters and, literally, sisters sawn in half.

ru.note: Russian 'сводные сёстры' has no 'half' in it.

en.note: 'Half-sisters' works literally in English.

gist: A light bulb tired of hanging around 'burns through', meaning both burning out and running off.

characters.looks: cartoon light bulb hanging from a cord, bored face

wordplay.explanation: German 'durchbrennen' means both a bulb burning out and someone running away.

ru.note: 'Перегорела' works for bulb and for losing motivation.

en.note: 'Burned out' works for bulb and exhaustion.

gist: IKEA has floor arrows because it is an 'Einrichtungshaus', read as both furniture store and one-way house.

wordplay.explanation: 'Einrichtungshaus' means furniture store, but also reads as 'one-direction house' (ein Richtung).

gist: A civil servant wonders why people complain about them since 'we don't do anything', meaning both harmless and idle.

characters.looks: bored clerk, cardigan, coffee mug, feet on desk
sleepy clerk, glasses, rubber stamp

wordplay.explanation: 'Wir tun doch nichts' means both 'we mean no harm' and 'we do no work'.

cultureRefs: German stereotype of lazy civil servants (Beamte)

ru.note: 'Мы же ничего не делаем' keeps both meanings.

en.note: 'We're not doing anything' keeps both meanings.

gist: Teacher with his 'third class' of pupils lets trains pass for hours because they only offer 1st and 2nd class, then gives up.

characters.looks: exhausted teacher, glasses, clipboard, frazzled hair
group of bored small schoolkids with backpacks

wordplay.explanation: 'Klasse' is both a school grade and a train class.

ru.note: Russian trains rarely label classes; frame as 'вагоны 1 и 2 класса'.

en.note: Call the group 'class 3' so it clashes with 1st/2nd class carriages.

gist: Anti-joke: what's yellow and lies in the water? An excavator; the excavator driver did not find it funny either.

characters.looks: soaked worker, hard hat, glum face

characters.looks: worried man, pajamas under coat, messy hair
calm doctor, white coat, stethoscope

gist: A billiard game without balls is 'neither half nor whole', because German calls striped and solid balls halves and wholes.

gist: Lifeguard scolds a man for peeing in the pool, the man says everyone does, the lifeguard says not from the 3-meter diving board.

gist: Yoda asked about the Leaning Tower of Pisa answers 'Gerade nicht', meaning both 'not right now' and 'not straight'.

characters.looks: reporter with microphone, press badge

wordplay.explanation: German 'gerade nicht' means both 'not right now' and 'not straight'.

ru.note: Russian 'прямо' means straight and 'прямо сейчас' right now; build the answer on that.

gist: The longest musical instrument is a cable drum, punning on drum.

en.note: 'Cable drum' keeps the pun.

gist: Customer at a kebab shop corrects 'mit alles' to 'mit allem', and the vendor says Allem has the day off, treating it as a name.
